newsitem.title: UK: UK royals seek to fill gap as youngsters desert.
newsitem.headline: UK royals seek to fill gap as youngsters desert.

text.p: Buckingham Palace said on Thursday it was exploring ways to fill the void left by some of Britain's younger royals, who have largely shunned the family business and opted for a life of fun over good works.

"We are looking to see if we can fill the gap," said a spokeswoman. "For other members of the royal family to take on extra (charitable work) depends on their own commitments. But there are a lot of members of the royal family so we will look across the board."

Go-it-alone family members such as Princess Diana and Sarah Ferguson have made clear their interests principally lie elsewhere, leaving other family members with little option but to pick up the slack or turn their back on scores of charities.
The very youngest royals, who are the Queen's grandchildren, are too young to take on much work and many of their older relatives already have a jam-packed schedule.
But the palace wants to ensure the royal family's charitable profile remains high given the never-ending stream of bad news -- hence the plan to redistribute the royal duties.

"This is a huge shift. The Queen can't be everywhere at once so she will call on lots of nice relations to help out and represent her. Some will do more, some less, some will continue to do abolutely nothing," said Harold Brooks-Baker of Burke's Peerage, the authoritative guide to Britain's aristocracy.

"Prince Edward, for example, will do very little indeed as he has so many other interests while the Duke of York (Prince Andrew) will do more and more," he said. "Much too much has fallen on a handful of people and the Queen would certainly have two or three dozen people to call on if she wished."
With only so many royals to go around, the palace said some charities might just have to accept their loss.
"The Queen has over 800 patronages...We can't cover every single charity so some might lose out," she said.
The main problem, yet again, is Princess Diana.

With her divorce from Prince Charles, the House of Windsor lost one of its most popular figures. Diana dropped many of her public engagements and cut down her patronage of charities, retaining links with only a favoured few good causes.

Instead of presiding over an endless round of formal functions, she has opted for more idiosyncratic do-gooding, visiting hospital wards undercover by night or attending operations, complete with surgical mask and onlooking cameras.
The shift in style has ensured her continued press coverage, even as the loyal royals toil on without a reporter in sight.
"Obviously with some of the princess's charities, if they're seeking a new patron they will be looked at," said the palace.
Prince Andrew, too, has seen his marriage collapse and the unpredictable Fergie, his ex-wife, has redirected her energies into making money -- for herself rather than charity.

Prince Edward, the queen's youngest child, is caught up in his own production business and has no wife with whom to share the burdens. Pressure is said to be mounting on the bachelor boy to wed and bring fresh blood into the family business.
Princess Anne, the queen's only daughter and arguably her most loyal servant, has stayed true to the family calling.
Anne carries out more public duties than any other family member, without a complaint, always with apparent interest -- if not much in the way of a smile -- and writes her own speeches.
Anne is estimated to shake 25,000 hands a year. No fashion icon, she changes her clothes 30 times a week when on duty.

"She has become the most prized royal of that generation. Considering that 15 years ago she was much disliked, all members of the royal family would be well instructed to turn to her on PR. If she can do it, they can surely do it," said Brooks-Baker.
As for less industrious royals, the palace denied reports that the queen's younger sister, Princess Margaret, would start working harder and pick up where the younger women left off.
In last year's list of royal engagements, Margaret was reported to have carried out 114 engagements compared with 514 by Anne, 509 by the Queen, and 417 by the Prince of Wales.
